title: Pygmalion
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Pygmalion, offended by the women he has watched living out their lives in crime, keeps to himself without a wife until he carves an ivory figure so lifelike that he falls in love with it, brings it gifts, dresses it, speaks to it and lays it on his bed. At Venus' festival he prays, obliquely, for a wife like his ivory girl; the goddess understands what he did not dare say, the ivory warms and softens under his hands, and the woman he made becomes his wife and bears a daughter, Paphos.

sentences.t:
Quas quia Pygmalion aevum per crimen agentes
viderat, offensus vitiis, quae plurima menti
femineae natura dedit, sine coniuge caelebs
vivebat thalamique diu consorte carebat.
sentences.l: And since Pygmalion had seen these [women] passing their life through crime, offended by the vices which nature gave in great number to the female mind, he was living unmarried, without a wife, and long went without a sharer of his marriage-chamber.
sentences.i: Pygmalion had watched them living their lives out in crime, and, offended by the vices nature has given the female mind in such abundance, he stayed unmarried, wifeless, and for a long time had no one to share his bed.
sentences.n: Quas is a connecting relative — “and these women” — picking up an antecedent that lies before this part; Latin keeps the link where English wants a new sentence, and the literal supplies “these [women].” Quas is the object of viderat, and agentes agrees with it: aevum agere is “to pass one's life.” Offensus takes the ablative of cause, vitiis. Plurima agrees with quae and works predicatively — the vices nature gave are very many — which is how both layers put it, “in great number” and “in such abundance.” Caelebs is “unmarried, single,” and is not English “celibate”: it says nothing about abstinence, and Ovid doubles it with sine coniuge for weight. Carere in the last clause governs the ablative, consorte.

sentences.t:
Interea niveum mira feliciter arte
sculpsit ebur formamque dedit, qua femina nasci
nulla potest: operisque sui concepit amorem.
sentences.l: Meanwhile with marvellous art he successfully carved snow-white ivory and gave it a form with which no woman can be born: and he conceived love of his own work.
sentences.i: Meanwhile, with marvellous skill and with success, he carved snow-white ivory and gave it a beauty no woman is born with; and he fell in love with his own work.
sentences.n: The adjective niveum sits in 247 and its noun ebur stands second in 248, so the phrase is split across the line-end, which Latin allows freely and English cannot imitate; mira and arte are pulled apart around feliciter inside 247. Feliciter is “with happy result, successfully,” not “cheerfully.” Qua is ablative and looks back to formam: forma is the shape or form a thing is given, and it shades into “beauty,” which is what the idiomatic takes up where the literal keeps “a form.” Operis sui is an objective genitive with amorem — the love is directed at the work.

sentences.t:
Virginis est verae facies, quam vivere credas,
et, si non obstet reverentia, velle moveri:
ars adeo latet arte sua.
sentences.l: It has the face of a true girl, one whom you would believe to be alive and, if modesty did not stand in the way, to wish to be moved: so far does art lie hidden by its own art.
sentences.i: It is a real girl's face — you would think her alive, and think that, if modesty did not hold her back, she would want to move: so completely is the art hidden by its own art.
sentences.n: Credas is a potential subjunctive with an indefinite “you” — anyone would believe it. Both infinitives, vivere and velle moveri, depend on credas; moveri is passive, “to be moved,” where English naturally hears “to move,” and the idiomatic follows English. Reverentia is best taken as the figure's own modesty, holding her still. Ars adeo latet arte sua is a tag-line built on the repeated noun: art so good that it hides the fact of being art, with arte sua the ablative of means by which it hides.

sentences.t:
Miratur et haurit
pectore Pygmalion simulati corporis ignes.
sentences.l: Pygmalion marvels and draws into his breast the fires of the counterfeited body.
sentences.i: Pygmalion marvels, and drinks into his breast the fire of the counterfeit body.
sentences.n: The two verbs miratur and haurit stand at the end of 252 and the subject Pygmalion arrives only in 253 — the name is held back across the line-end. Miratur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, and both layers render it active, “marvels.” Pectore is an ablative with haurit, the breast as the thing he draws with; the literal puts it as “into his breast,” because that is where English wants the fire to go. Haurire is the verb used of swallowing and drinking down. Ignes, plural, is the ordinary language of passion. Simulati corporis is a genitive with ignes — the fires belong to the body that has been counterfeited, and simulare is “to feign, to make a likeness of.”

sentences.t:
Saepe manus operi temptantes admovet, an sit
corpus an illud ebur: nec adhuc ebur esse fatetur.
sentences.l: Often he brings testing hands to the work, [wondering] whether it is a body or whether that is ivory: and he does not yet admit that it is ivory.
sentences.i: Again and again he lays his hands on the work to try it, to see whether it is flesh or whether it is ivory; and still he will not admit that it is ivory.
sentences.n: Temptantes is a present participle agreeing with manus — hands that test, that try by touch. An ... an is an indirect double question, “whether ... or,” with the subjunctive sit; the verb of asking is left to be understood and the literal supplies “[wondering].” The point is in the last clause: nec ... fatetur, he does not admit it, which is not the same as not knowing. Temptare recurs at 282, 283 and 289 — the same testing hand each time.

sentences.t:
Oscula dat reddique putat loquiturque tenetque,
et credit tactis digitos insidere membris,
et metuit, pressos veniat ne livor in artus.
sentences.l: He gives kisses and thinks them given back, and speaks to it and holds it, and believes that his fingers sink into the limbs he touches, and fears that a bruise may come upon the limbs he has pressed.
sentences.i: He kisses it and believes the kiss returned; he talks to it, holds it, feels his fingers sink into the limbs he touches, and is afraid a bruise will rise where he has pressed.
sentences.n: The three -que's of 256 (reddique, loquiturque, tenetque) pile the actions up without a pause. Reddi is a passive infinitive with putat — he thinks the kisses are being given back. Membris is dative with insidere, “sink into.” In the last clause ne is postponed behind its own verb (veniat ne), and the adjective pressos is separated from its noun artus by the words between; both are ordinary in verse. The fear is the fear you would have for a living body.

sentences.t:
Et modo blanditias adhibet, modo grata puellis
munera fert illi conchas teretesque lapillos
et parvas volucres et flores mille colorum
liliaque pictasque pilas et ab arbore lapsas
Heliadum lacrimas;
sentences.l: And now he applies blandishments, now he brings her gifts welcome to girls: shells and smooth pebbles and small birds and flowers of a thousand colours and lilies and painted balls and, fallen from the tree, the tears of the Heliades;
sentences.i: And now he plies her with endearments, now he brings her the presents girls like: seashells, smooth pebbles, little birds, flowers of a thousand colours, lilies, painted balls, and amber, the tears of the Heliades, fallen from the tree.
sentences.n: Modo ... modo is “now ... now,” marking the alternation. Blanditiae are coaxing, flattering words together with the caresses that go with them, so the literal's “blandishments” and the idiomatic's “endearments” are two sides of the one word. Grata puellis is an adjective with the dative — gifts girls find welcome; illi is a separate dative, the recipient, the ivory girl. Everything from conchas onward is accusative in apposition to munera: a long list held together by nothing but case. Heliadum lacrimas, “the tears of the Heliades,” is a periphrasis for amber — the sisters of Phaethon were turned into trees, and their weeping hardened into it. The literal keeps the periphrasis and the idiomatic unpacks it.

sentences.t:
ornat quoque vestibus artus,
dat digitis gemmas, dat longa monilia collo:
sentences.l: he also adorns her limbs with clothes, gives gems to her fingers, gives long necklaces to her neck:
sentences.i: he dresses her limbs as well, sets jewels on her fingers and hangs long necklaces at her throat.
sentences.n: Quoque here is the adverb “also,” not the ablative quo with the enclitic -que — a trap worth naming, since the two are written the same; at 282 manibus quoque is again the adverb. Vestibus is an ablative of means with ornat. Digitis and collo are datives of the person or thing to which, where English says “on” and “at.” The repeated dat, twice in one line, keeps the giving going.

sentences.t: aure leves bacae, redimicula pectore pendent.
sentences.l: at her ear light pearls, ribbons at her breast, hang.
sentences.i: Light pearls hang at her ears, ribbons across her breast.
sentences.n: One verb, pendent, serves both halves of the line, and the first half has no verb of its own. Aure and pectore are ablatives of place where, with no preposition — normal in verse. Baca is literally a berry, used of a pearl for its shape. Redimicula are trailing bands or ribbons, the ties and streamers of a headdress or a garment. The line is chiastic — aure leves bacae, then redimicula pectore — so the two ablatives stand at the outside and the two nominatives in the middle, and the literal follows that order.

sentences.t: Cuncta decent: nec nuda minus formosa videtur.
sentences.l: All things become [her]: nor does she seem less beautiful naked.
sentences.i: It all suits her; and naked she seems no less beautiful.
sentences.n: Decent is plural with cuncta as its subject: Latin says “all things are becoming,” and the person they suit is left unexpressed, so the literal supplies “[her].” Nuda is a nominative feminine adjective agreeing with the unexpressed subject of videtur, and it carries the weight of an English clause — “when she is naked.” Minus goes with formosa, not with videtur.

sentences.t:
Conlocat hanc stratis concha Sidonide tinctis
appellatque tori sociam,
sentences.l: He lays her down on coverlets dyed with the Sidonian shell, and calls her the partner of his couch,
sentences.i: He settles her on bedclothes dyed with the purple of the Sidonian shell and calls her the companion of his bed,
sentences.n: Concha Sidonis is the murex of Sidon, the shellfish from which the famous purple dye was taken; Sidonide is a Greek ablative ending, borrowed with the Greek name. Strata are the spread bedclothes, ablative of place where without a preposition. Tori sociam is a predicative accusative with appellat — he calls her the partner of the couch, which is what a wife is called.

sentences.t:
acclinataque colla
mollibus in plumis, tamquam sensura, reponit.
sentences.l: and her leaned-back neck he lays on soft feathers, as though [it, or she] were going to feel.
sentences.i: and lays her tilted-back neck on soft down, as though she would feel it.
sentences.n: Colla is a poetic plural for one neck. Acclinata is a perfect participle agreeing with colla — the neck is already tilted back as he sets it down. Sensura is a future participle, “going to feel,” and its ending is formally two things at once: neuter plural, agreeing with colla, and feminine singular, agreeing with the girl herself. The one word it cannot agree with is Pygmalion, who is masculine. The literal holds both readings open with a bracketed “[it, or she]” — a pronoun the Latin does not have and English cannot do without — and the idiomatic picks the girl. Sensura has no object in the Latin either; the idiomatic supplies “it.” Tamquam marks the whole gesture as pretence.

sentences.t:
Festa dies Veneris tota celeberrima Cypro
venerat,
sentences.l: The festal day of Venus, most thronged in all Cyprus, had come,
sentences.i: Venus' festival day had come, the most crowded in all Cyprus,
sentences.n: Celeber means “thronged, well-attended” before it means “famous,” so celeberrima is the busiest day of the year, not merely the best known. Tota Cypro is an ablative of place where without a preposition. Cyprus is Venus' own island; at 297 an island takes its name from Pygmalion's daughter. Venerat is pluperfect: the day has already arrived when the sentence begins.

sentences.t:
et pandis inductae cornibus aurum
conciderant ictae nivea cervice iuvencae,
turaque fumabant:
sentences.l: and the heifers, gold drawn over their spreading horns, had fallen, struck on the snow-white neck, and the incense was smoking:
sentences.i: and the heifers had gone down, their curved horns sheathed in gold, struck on their snow-white necks, and the incense was smoking:
sentences.n: Inductae is a passive participle that keeps an accusative object, aurum — the Greek construction in which a passive participle governs an accusative of respect, “having gold drawn over them,” with pandis cornibus the place it is drawn over. It is the same idiom as “veiled as to her face.” Nivea cervice is an ablative, the place of the blow, with ictae. Conciderant is pluperfect and fumabant imperfect: the killing is already done, the incense is still burning, when Pygmalion arrives.

sentences.t:
cum munere functus ad aras
constitit et timide, “si di dare cuncta potestis,
sit coniunx, opto” (non ausus “eburnea virgo”
dicere) Pygmalion “similis mea” dixit “eburnae.”
sentences.l: when, having discharged his offering, he took his stand at the altars and timidly — “If you gods can give all things, let my wife be, I pray” (not having dared to say “the ivory girl”) — Pygmalion said — “like the ivory one.”
sentences.i: when, his offering discharged, he stood at the altars and said, timidly, “If you gods can give all things, I pray my wife may be” — he did not dare to say “the ivory girl” — “like the ivory one.”
sentences.n: Munere functus: fungor is deponent, passive in form and active in meaning, and takes the ablative munere — “having discharged the offering.” Non ausus is from audeo, semi-deponent: passive in form in the perfect, active in sense, “not having dared.” Si ... potestis is a plain condition with the indicative; sit is best taken as a jussive subjunctive, “let her be,” with opto dropped in as a parenthesis, though opto can also govern a subjunctive without ut, and the sense is the same either way. The prayer is deliberately oblique: he asks for a wife similis eburnae, like the ivory one, and not for the ivory girl herself, and the parenthesis says outright that he did not dare name what he wanted. Mea is printed inside the second fragment of the speech but belongs with coniunx in the first — “my wife.” It is nominative, and cannot agree with eburnae, which is dative after similis; so neither layer may read “my ivory one,” and both give “my wife” in the first fragment and “like the ivory one” in the second.

sentences.t:
Sensit, ut ipsa suis aderat Venus aurea festis,
vota quid illa velint;
sentences.l: She understood — as golden Venus herself was present at her own festival — what those prayers wanted;
sentences.i: Golden Venus was there in person at her own festival, and she understood what that prayer meant;
sentences.n: Ut with the indicative aderat is “as, seeing that” — a temporal-causal ut, not purpose or result. Sensit stands first with no subject expressed; the subject Venus arrives only inside the ut-clause, and the object of sensit — the indirect question vota quid illa velint, with its subjunctive velint — waits until the next line. Quid velint is the idiom “what they mean, what they are getting at,” and that is the whole point of the scene: she hears past what he actually said.

sentences.t:
et, amici numinis omen,
flamma ter accensa est apicemque per aera duxit.
sentences.l: and — an omen of a favouring divinity — the flame was kindled three times and drew a point up through the air.
sentences.i: and, as a sign that the god was favourable, the flame flared three times and drew a tongue of fire up through the air.
sentences.n: Amici numinis omen is an accusative standing in apposition to the whole action that follows: the flaring itself is the omen. Numen is the divine power at work rather than the person of the goddess. Ter, three times, is the ritual number that makes a sign unmistakable. Accensa est is passive — the flame “was kindled,” by an agent the line does not name. Apex is the point or peak of a flame, and aera is the Greek accusative of aer.

sentences.t:
Ut rediit, simulacra suae petit ille puellae
incumbensque toro dedit oscula: visa tepere est.
sentences.l: When he came back, he sought the image of his own girl and, leaning on the couch, gave it kisses: she seemed to be warm.
sentences.i: When he came back he went to his girl's likeness and, leaning over the bed, kissed it: she seemed warm.
sentences.n: Ut rediit is ut with the perfect indicative in its plain temporal sense, “when he returned” — a different ut from the one at 277. Simulacra is a poetic plural for one statue. The unexpressed subject of visa ... est is singular and cannot be the neuter plural simulacra: the sentence has quietly changed subject to the girl herself, though the Latin goes back to calling her ebur at 283 and reaches corpus only at 289. Tepere is “to be lukewarm,” the first degree of warmth, and it is what he feels through his lips.

sentences.t: Admovet os iterum, manibus quoque pectora temptat:
sentences.l: He brings his mouth to her again; with his hands too he tries her breast:
sentences.i: He puts his mouth to her again, and with his hands as well he tries her breast.
sentences.n: Admovet and temptat are present where the surrounding narrative has been in past tenses — the historic present, which pulls the moment up close and holds it. Os is the mouth. Quoque is again the adverb “also,” as at 263, not quo with -que. Pectora is a poetic plural. Temptat picks up the temptantes of 254 and is picked up in turn at 283 and 289.

sentences.t:
temptatum mollescit ebur positoque rigore
subsidit digitis ceditque,
sentences.l: the ivory, tried, grows soft and, its stiffness laid aside, sinks beneath his fingers and gives way,
sentences.i: the ivory he tries goes soft, its stiffness gone, and sinks under his fingers and yields,
sentences.n: Temptatum is a perfect participle agreeing with ebur — the ivory that has been tried. Posito rigore is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with its stiffness laid aside,” where English would ordinarily use a clause; the literal keeps the participle. Digitis is dative with subsidit, “gives way to the fingers,” which the literal renders “beneath his fingers.” Mollescit, and remollescit at 285, are inceptive verbs in -sco: “begins to be soft.” The softening is a process, not an event.

sentences.t:
ut Hymettia sole
cera remollescit tractataque pollice multas
flectitur in facies ipsoque fit utilis usu.
sentences.l: as Hymettian wax grows soft again in the sun and, worked by the thumb, is bent into many shapes and by the very handling becomes fit for use.
sentences.i: the way wax from Hymettus softens again in the sun and, worked under the thumb, is bent into many shapes and made useful by the very handling.
sentences.n: Hymettus is the mountain in Attica famous for its bees, so Hymettia cera is simply beeswax, named from its best-known source. Sole is a bare ablative naming what does the softening, which English can only put as “in the sun.” Tractata is a passive participle with pollice as its ablative of means, and flectitur is passive too — the wax is worked, it does not shape itself. Facies here is “shapes, forms,” not “faces.” Ipso usu is “by the very handling”: the working that softens it is the same working that makes it good for anything.

sentences.t:
Dum stupet et dubie gaudet fallique veretur,
rursus amans rursusque manu sua vota retractat.
sentences.l: While he is stunned and rejoices doubtfully and fears to be deceived, the lover handles again and again with his hand what he has prayed for.
sentences.i: Stunned, hesitantly glad, afraid of being deceived, the lover goes over what he prayed for again and again with his hand.
sentences.n: Dum with the present indicative is “while,” and the three presents hold the whole line in one moment. Veretur is deponent, passive in form and active in sense, and the literal renders it active, “fears”; falli beside it is a genuine passive infinitive, “to be deceived.” Rursus ... rursusque doubles the adverb for the repetition of the gesture. Vota are the things prayed for, not the words of the prayer, so what his hand goes over is the answer itself; retractat is “handles again,” from the same root as the tractata of 285.

sentences.t: Corpus erat: saliunt temptatae pollice venae.
sentences.l: It was a body: the veins, tried by the thumb, leap.
sentences.i: It was flesh: the veins leap when the thumb tries them.
sentences.n: Corpus erat answers the question left open at 254 to 255, an sit corpus an illud ebur; the imperfect erat states it flatly and without comment. Saliunt is present after that imperfect — the pulse is happening now, in front of us. Temptatae is a perfect participle agreeing with venae, and pollice is an ablative of means: the same testing thumb as at 285, which there worked wax and here finds a pulse.

sentences.t:
Tum vero Paphius plenissima concipit heros
verba, quibus Veneri grates agat, oraque tandem
ore suo non falsa premit:
sentences.l: Then indeed the Paphian hero conceives the fullest words with which he might give Venus thanks, and at last presses with his own mouth a mouth that is not false:
sentences.i: Then indeed the hero of Paphos puts together the fullest words, words with which to give Venus thanks, and presses his own mouth at last to a mouth that is not false.
sentences.n: Paphius heros names Pygmalion from the place, ahead of the daughter Paphos who is born at 297 and gives the name. The adjective plenissima sits inside 290 and its noun verba opens 291, so the phrase is stretched across the line-end; Paphius and heros are pulled apart around the verb in the same line. Concipit verba is “frames words, puts words together,” the same verb as concepit amorem at 249. Quibus ... agat is a relative clause with the subjunctive, expressing purpose: words with which to give thanks. Ora and ore are the plural and singular of one word, mouth: oraque stands near the end of 291 and ore opens 292, so the two forms meet across the line-end — his own mouth against a mouth that is now non falsa.

sentences.t:
dataque oscula virgo
sensit et erubuit timidumque ad lumina lumen
attollens pariter cum caelo vidit amantem.
sentences.l: and the girl felt the kisses that had been given, and blushed, and, raising a timid light to the light, saw her lover together with the sky.
sentences.i: and the girl felt the kisses given her, and blushed, and, lifting a timid eye to the daylight, saw her lover and the sky in the same moment.
sentences.n: Data oscula is a perfect participle with its noun — “the kisses [that had been] given” — packing into a participle what English makes a clause. Timidum lumen and ad lumina are the same word twice: lumen is both the eye and the light it opens on, so she raises her light to the light, and the literal keeps the play where the idiomatic separates the two senses. Pariter cum caelo, “equally with the sky,” means the two sights arrive together: the first thing she ever sees is daylight and the man at once. Attollens is a present participle agreeing with virgo.

sentences.t: Coniugio, quod fecit, adest dea.
sentences.l: At the marriage which she made, the goddess is present.
sentences.i: The goddess attends the marriage she has made.
sentences.n: Adsum takes the dative, coniugio — “is present at.” Quod is neuter, agreeing with coniugio, and the subject of fecit is the goddess: she both made the match and attends it. Adest is present in a narrative of past tenses, the historic present again, holding the scene open.

sentences.t:
Iamque coactis
cornibus in plenum noviens lunaribus orbem
illa Paphon genuit, de qua tenet insula nomen.
sentences.l: And now, with the moon's horns drawn together nine times into a full circle, she bore Paphos, from whom the island holds its name.
sentences.i: And now the moon's horns had closed nine times into a full disc, and she gave birth to Paphos, from whom the island takes its name.
sentences.n: Coactis ... cornibus lunaribus is an ablative absolute — “with the moon's horns drawn together” — which the literal keeps as a participle and the idiomatic turns into a clause. Noviens, nine times, counts the nine months: each closing of the crescent into a full disc is one month. Paphon is a Greek accusative. De qua is feminine, so the child is a daughter. Ovid writes insula, the island, and derives its name from her.
